## Q1. Summary statistics

```{r}
summary_stats <- function(values) {
  c(n = sum(!is.na(values)), mean = mean(values, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(values, na.rm = TRUE), sd = sd(values, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(values, na.rm = TRUE), max = max(values, na.rm = TRUE))
}

summary_stats(mtcars$mpg)
```

## Q2. Two sample t test

```{r}
t_test_two <- function(group1, group2) {
  se1 <- var(group1) / length(group1)
  se2 <- var(group2) / length(group2)
  t_stat <- (mean(group1) - mean(group2)) / sqrt(se1 + se2)
  df <- (se1 + se2)^2 / (se1^2/(length(group1)-1) + se2^2/(length(group2)-1))
  p_val <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df)
  list(t = t_stat, df = df, p_value = p_val)
}

manual_mpg <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 1]
auto_mpg   <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 0]

t_test_two(manual_mpg, auto_mpg)
t.test(manual_mpg, auto_mpg)
```

## Q3. The apply family

The apply family runs one function over many pieces of data, so you don't need a loop. Peng's book explains these in the chapter on loop functions.

### lapply

`lapply` runs a function on each item of a list (or each column of a data frame). The answer is always a list.

```{r}
lapply(mtcars[, c("mpg", "hp")], mean)
```

### sapply

`sapply` does the same as `lapply`, but tries to make the answer simpler, like a vector. It is easier to read.

```{r}
sapply(mtcars[, c("mpg", "hp")], mean)
```

### tapply

`tapply` splits the values into groups, then runs the function on each group. Here the groups are the number of cylinders.

```{r}
tapply(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$cyl, mean)
```

### mapply

`mapply` takes two or more vectors and runs the function on the first items together, then the second items together, and so on. It works like a loop over several inputs.

```{r}
mapply(function(a, b) a + b, 1:3, 4:6)
```

### apply

`apply` runs a function on each row or column of a matrix or data frame. `2` means columns, `1` means rows.

```{r}
apply(mtcars[, 1:3], 2, max)      # max of each column
apply(mtcars[1:5, 1:3], 1, sum)   # sum of each row
```
